newsitem.title: USA: NYS Gov sees no progress in rent control fight.
newsitem.headline: NYS Gov sees no progress in rent control fight.

text.p: New York State Gov George Pataki on Tuesday told reporters in Albany he had yet to make headway with legislative leaders in resolving a major fight over apartment rent rules that expire on Sunday.

Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, who has taken the toughest stand in the battle, and repeatedly said he would let the regulations expire on Sunday if no accord were reached with the Democrat Assembly, softened his stance.
Asked whether the Senate would approve its own bill on Sunday, he replied "We might not." Bruno wants the rules ended gradually while protecting the needy, elderly and disabled.

Saying he had enough votes to get a rent rule bill approved by the Senate, Bruno left open when it might be voted on by that house's Republican majority. "We will draw a bill, and I will be prepared to pass a bill with whatever votes it takes in the Majority to pass it. But whether I put it out or not, I'm going to just reflect on that for awhile," said Bruno, linking his decision to whether the Democrat Minority Leader introduced what Bruno called "disruptive" amendments.
Republican Senators from Manhattan, which has the vast majority of the state's rent-regulated apartments, are concerned the Senate's bill might jeopardize their chances for re-election.

While Pataki noted different options were being disucssed, he did not elaborate on them, adding: "But I don't see at the present time a way to bridge the differences, unless we put aside the politics and look at the real goal, and the real goal is very simple, and that is to protect the tenants, and the plan that I've outlined does that."

The Republican governor's plan includes vacancy decontrol, which Assembly Speaker Silver, D-Manhattan, opposes, saying it would end the regulations over time and subject tenants to harrassment by their landlords.

The New York Times said one option being discussed was raising by five to 10 percent the nine-percent bonus landlords now get when a tenant leaves a regulated apartment, or letting landlords raise rents on vacant apartments to market rates and then limiting future rises as long as the tenant stays in the same apartment.

Pataki, who had planned to attend a fund-raiser at the Meadow Brook Golf Club in Jericho, on Long Island, said he would again meet with lawmakers later this afternoon but left open the possibility he would attend the outing on Wednesday.

The event has proved controversial as it was organized in part by Charles Urstadt, a real estate executive, who in 1971, when he was Commissioner of Housing and Community Renewal, helped push a vacancy decontrol bill through the legislature, according to the New York Times.

The bill was repealed in 1974 amid reports that landlords were trying to harrass tenants so that they would leave their apartments, allowing free-market prices to be charged instead of the lower, regulated ones.

The governor and top lawmakers plan to resume their session with meetings on crime, complying with the federal truth in sentencing law, welfare, and education. But little progress was expected on these issues until the negotiations over rent rules concluded. New York State's budget was due on April 1, and that pact also has been delayed by the fight over rent regulations.
The Assembly Speaker was expected to observe a religious holiday from sundown on Tuesday through Thursday, which would make him unavailable for talks during that period.
The legislature also was expected to meet on Sunday evening.
